Andrew Ng · AI Engineering Skills Map: Using coding agents · Andrew Ng · Writing Agent Project Engineering Lifecycle: from demo to maintainable system §8. P Calling a model and tools only proves that an execution path exists. A maintainable Agent project also needs a task contract, repository conventions, runtime topology, capability contracts, state lifecycles, evaluation evidence, and production feedback. FIG. 8. P1 · AGENT PROJECT ENGINEERING LIFECYCLE Ten teaching steps collapse into five engineering phases This is not a one-way waterfall. Evals, traces, and production failures can route work back to the earliest incorrect layer. DEFINE Task Contract + Repository Contract + Architecture Goal · Input · Output · Boundary · Success Criteria; then define repository conventions, validation commands, dependency/secret rules, module responsibilities, and failure paths. BUILD Agent · Tools · Skills · Context / Memory · Prompt Agents handle uncertain decisions; workflows own explicit control; tools expose single capabilities; skills encode methods; state/memory manage information lifecycles; prompts become versioned behavior configuration. VERIFY Test + Eval Tests validate program contracts; evals validate task behavior. A fixed dataset makes model, prompt, skill, and workflow versions genuinely comparable. OPERATE Deploy · Trace · Monitor Connect request, workflow state, Agent decisions, tool I/O, versions, tokens, latency, cost, and task outcome into one diagnosable execution path. LEARN ↺ Root Cause → Dataset → Fix → Regression Production evidence should return to the earliest wrong layer: fix state when state is wrong, fix tools when tools fail, fix stale sources when evidence is stale—not every problem belongs in the prompt. Engineering goal Make uncertain model behavior reliably serve a bounded, testable, observable business task. FIG. 8. P2 · RESPONSIBILITY BOUNDARIES Do not call every responsibility an Agent Long-term maintainability comes from responsibility boundaries: who decides, who executes, who stores state, and who verifies success. Component Owns Should not silently own Workflow Order, branching, retries, fallback, stopping Open-ended business judgment Agent Uncertain judgment, planning, diagnosis, selection Implicit ownership of all flow and authority Tool A single testable external operation A full task procedure Skill A validated reusable task method Protocol transport or final authorization Context / State Task-relevant information and execution state Unlimited transcript accumulation Memory Curated durable information Every temporary result and error Test / Eval Program contracts + task-behavior evidence Judging improvement by intuition Repository instructions Coding-agent repository instructions should stay concise and point to the real architecture, test, and product documentation. Codex officially supports AGENTS. md, but that filename is not a universal standard across all Agent tools. FIG. 8. P3 · AGENT ENGINEER CAPABILITY STACK The differentiator is not framework count, but turning a business objective into an operable system Four capability layers form one loop: business defines the objective, architecture carries execution, reliability supplies evidence, and delivery keeps the system evolving. 1 · BUSINESS Business decomposition & workflow design KPI · current workflow · automation boundary · human gate · exception path · Task Contract. Ask what success means before choosing a framework. 2 · ARCHITECTURE Runtime & capability architecture Tool / schema · Workflow · Agent · State · Context · Memory · Routing · Permission · failure semantics 3 · RELIABILITY Evaluation, observability & reliability task success · tool failure · latency · cost/success · human escalation · trace · alert · fallback · regression gate 4 · DELIVERY Engineering delivery & continuous iteration versioning · CI/CD · environment separation · rollout · rollback · runbook · incident diagnosis · production learning BUSINESS PROBLEM "Support cost is too high" Translate first into bounded outcomes, KPIs, and automation boundaries. SYSTEM Task Contract → Runtime Architecture Choose workflow, agent, tools, and state; do not let the framework define the business problem backwards. EVIDENCE Eval → Trace → Release Gate Prove task success, failure location, cost, and risk instead of relying on intuition. PRODUCTION LEARNING ↺ Operate → Diagnose → Regression → Improve Production reveals the real failure distribution; route evidence back to the earliest incorrect layer. Capability boundary Agent engineering competence is the ability to turn an ambiguous business objective into a bounded, testable, observable, operable system. Version compatibility Do not assume prompts remain compatible after a model upgrade; run a fixed regression suite and compare task success, safety, latency, and cost. Agent Architecture Selection: patterns, not seven maturity tiers §8. AS Single Agent, ReAct, Plan & Execute, Multi-Agent, Route + Skill, Shared State, and Graph Workflow are not mutually exclusive architectures on one axis. Production systems usually compose them; control flow, state, permissions, recovery, cost, and latency drive the choice. FIG. 8. AS1 · AGENT ARCHITECTURE PATTERN SPACE The seven architectures actually span five control dimensions Do not ask which tier you belong to; ask which dimensions of your system need stronger control. ACTORS Single Agent ↔ Multi-Agent Decides how many independent decision makers are needed and whether real context, permission, tool, evaluation, or parallelism boundaries exist. DECISION ReAct ↔ Plan & Execute Choose between local step-by-step decisions and global decomposition followed by execution, verification, and replanning. CAPABILITY Router + Skill When capabilities are enumerable, bounded, and evaluable, reduce open-ended reasoning into explicit capability selection. STATE Shared State / Blackboard-like Multiple workers collaborate around shared work state, requiring typed state, ownership, merge/reducer rules, versioning, and conflict policy. CONTROL Graph / Durable Workflow When branch, join, loop, checkpoint, resume, HITL, recovery, and audit paths are application contracts, make the topology explicit. Composition rule Agent architectures are composable control patterns, not a maturity ladder. FIG. 8. AS2 · FAILURE-DRIVEN SELECTION Select control patterns from observed failure modes A new control structure is worth its complexity only when it solves an observed problem. Failure / requirement First pattern to consider Why Small tool set · short horizon Bounded Single Agent Minimum coordination overhead Next action depends on fresh observation ReAct-style loop Stepwise dynamic decisions Long task · global decomposition Plan & Execute Separate planning from execution and allow replanning Large known capability catalog Router + Skill Retrievable, authorizable, and evaluable Context / permission isolation Multi-Agent / Subgraph Real operational boundaries Shared work state conflicts Typed Shared State Explicit ownership, reducers, and versions Branch / join / loop / HITL Graph Workflow Control topology becomes application logic Crash must not restart the whole job Durable Workflow Runtime Recovery guarantees first Framework ≠ pattern LangGraph is stateful Agent orchestration; Temporal emphasizes durable workflow execution; Prefect is workflow orchestration; n8n is workflow automation. Choose runtimes by execution guarantees and integration model rather than labeling all of them Agent Graph frameworks. Multi-Agent Conflict Control: route disagreement into the control plane §8. R Production Multi-Agent systems do not aim for agents that never disagree. They classify conflicts into authority, quality, and resource conflicts, then resolve them with permissions, evidence, state machines, and concurrency control. FIG. 8. R1 · CONFLICT CONTROL MATRIX Classify the conflict before choosing a resolution mechanism Conflict type Actual question Weak default Production control Authority Who is authorized to decide the next step? Higher-ranked agent is automatically correct authority matrix · evidence · policy / human escalation Quality Does the artifact actually satisfy the acceptance criteria? Ask another Judge for one more opinion read-only verifier · reproducible evidence · bounded repair Resource Who may mutate shared resources, and when? Prompt everyone not to touch the same file ownership · isolation · CAS · merge / validation gate Voting boundary Three votes are not three independent observations. Count independent evidence before counting Agent opinions. FIG. 8. R2 · MULTI-AGENT HARNESS CONTROL Evidence → Authority → State Transition → Recovery Opinions may come from models, but execution authority, state transitions, and shared-resource mutation must be controlled explicitly by the harness. 01 Finding / Artifact Workers and specialists return conclusions together with evidence, uncertainty, artifact versions, and blocking risks. 02 Verifier Prefer tests, commands, and structured checks. Use a model judge only when contextual judgment is needed, returning PASS / FAIL / PARTIAL plus evidence. 03 Authority Gate The Lead may own orchestration authority, while truth authority comes from evidence. High-risk, unauthorized, or out-of-scope decisions route to a Policy or Human Gate. 04 State / Concurrency Gate Task DAGs, ownership, revision/CAS, write-scope warnings, workspace isolation, and merge gates constrain shared-state mutation. 05 Repair / Escalate / Complete Repair loops need an attempt budget. When the budget is exhausted, evidence is insufficient, or authority is missing, escalate explicitly instead of looping forever between reviewer and worker. DEEPSEEK HARNESS Current first-party material for the experimental Agent Teams supports a shared task DAG, monotonic revisions with CAS, Lead-only teammate lifecycle controls, and write-scope overlap warnings. But writeScopes are explicitly advisory rather than locks, and the default is a shared checkout with no automatic Git worktree creation. Final rule A reliable Multi-Agent system is not one where Agents rarely disagree; it is one where disagreement has a deterministic resolution path. FIG. 8. R3 · FOUR-LAYER CONSISTENCY MODEL Consistency is not model agreement; each of four layers needs explicit commit semantics Communication topology may be flexible, but the authoritative paths for state, execution, artifacts, and decisions must be inspectable, reject stale or duplicate work, and remain auditable. STATE CONSISTENCY One authoritative commit path authoritative store · versioned snapshot · revision/CAS · single writer / transaction / workflow engine. The key boundary is that a local view is not committed state. EXECUTION CONSISTENCY Duplicate delivery must not mean duplicate effect task id · lease · dedupe · idempotency · reconciliation. Locks address mutual exclusion; idempotency addresses duplicate business effects. They are different guarantees. ARTIFACT CONSISTENCY Candidate → Validate → Commit schema · provenance · lineage · integrity · acceptance. Parallel outputs are normalized, conflict-checked, and validated before a committed artifact is produced instead of being concatenated directly. DECISION CONSISTENCY Evidence + Authority + Policy Meaningful disagreement may remain. Deterministic verifiers, contextual judges, authority matrices, policy, and human escalation determine the committed action. Over-strong claim Production-grade rewrite Subagents must never communicate directly Agents may communicate, but not bypass authoritative state, policy, or side-effect commit paths Every agent must always see the latest data Specify consistency per boundary; sometimes one versioned snapshot is more correct A distributed lock prevents duplicates lock ≠ idempotency · dedupe · reconciliation A validator guarantees one uniquely correct answer Validators classify agreement, conflict, or insufficient evidence and may escalate Final rule Communication may be flexible; commit semantics must be explicit. Effective Agent Harness: Simplicity · Transparency · ACI §8. Z A strong agent is not the strongest model plus the most tools and the most complex framework. The model supplies capability; the harness determines how context, tools, state, environment feedback, validation, and human control convert that capability into reliable execution. FIG. 8. Z1 · EFFECTIVE AGENT PRINCIPLES Anthropic's three principles map directly to harness design questions SIMPLICITY Add complexity only for real failure modes single call → tool loop → workflow → graph → multi-agent. Each upgrade should solve a concrete state, recovery, permission, parallelism, or observability problem. TRANSPARENCY Expose Plan · Action · Evidence · State Transparency is not exposing hidden chain-of-thought. Make todos, tool calls, results, diffs, tests, retries, approvals, and completion evidence observable and steerable. ACI Agent-Computer Interface Tool names, schemas, parameter semantics, error models, and returned evidence are themselves prompt engineering. Repeated errors should first be attacked with interface constraints. FIG. 8. Z2 · HARNESS CONTROL LOOP Model output is not completion evidence; environment feedback closes the loop 1 Plan / Decide Choose the next step without treating the plan itself as ground truth. 2 Tool / Action Execute a bounded action through a clear ACI while the host and policy layer retain real authority. 3 Observe Ground Truth tool result · test · diff · browser observation · retrieval evidence · policy result 4 Update State / Verify Use real environment evidence to continue, repair, roll back, escalate, or stop. 5 Trace → Eval → ACI Repair Cluster repeated tool failures, repair names, schemas, defaults, error messages, or validation, then rerun regression evaluation. FIG. 8. Z3 · ACI / PI IMPLEMENTATION NOTES Keep implementation boundaries explicit instead of turning product details into universal laws Example Currently verified fact Reusable principle Pi Tool Surface default: read · bash · edit · write; prompt rules follow enabled tools Prompt inventory and executable capability inventory should not drift Pi edit unique oldText · same-original multi-edit · diff/patch evidence Move deterministic bookkeeping out of the model's action space Pi path relative OR absolute Do not turn a product implementation into a universal absolute-path rule Anthropic SWE-bench Tool relative-path errors → required absolute path Poka-yoke repeated failure at the interface Pi Session JSONL · id/parentId tree · compaction preserves raw history Audit history ≠ active model context ≠ summary Tool minimalism Minimize overlapping ways to express the same action. The goal is to reduce semantic overlap and choice ambiguity, not mechanically minimize tool count. Transparency boundary Expose plans, actions, state transitions, evidence, and concise reasoning summaries when useful. Do not make debugging or auditing depend on hidden chain-of-thought. FIG. 8. Z4 · HARNESS EVOLUTION As models get stronger, harness work does not simply disappear; it shifts from compensation to governance Some older scaffolding may move into the model or provider runtime, but greater autonomy, blast radius, and real-resource access increase the need for explicit permission, state, cost, audit, and recovery guarantees. COMPENSATORY HARNESS Compensate for model capability gaps format repair · rigid retry loops · weak-planning scaffolds · argument normalization · basic self-correction GOVERNANCE / RUNTIME HARNESS Govern stronger action capability permission · sandbox · durable state · budget · timeout · audit · approval · recovery · tenant boundary MODEL CAPABILITY ↑ Some compensating logic moves into the model, SDK, or provider runtime structured arguments · tool dispatch · handoffs · sessions · simple retry/self-correction · built-in shell/computer primitives AUTONOMY / BLAST RADIUS ↑ System guarantees become more important, not less Who may do what, whether state is durable, whether cost is bounded, how failures recover, and whether actions are auditable must all be owned by an explicit runtime contract. Question Model capability Harness guarantee Can it figure out the next step? planning / reasoning — Is it allowed to do it? — permission / policy / approval Can it resume after a crash? — state / checkpoint / reconciliation Can it consume unbounded cost? — budget / rate / timeout / cancellation Can failures be explained and audited? — observable trace / artifact / evidence Final rule Model improvement removes some scaffolding; it does not remove the need for runtime guarantees. TRACE BOUNDARY Trace observable trajectory—tool calls, handoffs, guardrails, state transitions, errors, artifacts, latency, and cost. Do not make private hidden chain-of-thought a required harness log. External verification date: 2026-09-28. Sources include Anthropic's Building Effective Agents, current Pi source and session documentation, Anthropic claude-cookbooks, 12-factor-agents, and OpenAI Harness Engineering. Product facts are implementation evidence; the core rules remain vendor-neutral. Long-Running Multi-Agent Handoff: validate before committing the handoff §8. S The key to long-running multi-agent work is not asking each agent to remember its own progress. Agents should be disposable while workflow state, validated artifacts, and legal state transitions remain durable. FIG. 8. S1 · DURABLE HANDOFF PROTOCOL Candidate ≠ committed artifact; an agent saying done ≠ a committed workflow transition 01 · READ Committed State + Versioned Inputs The worker reads durable workflow state, revision, ownership or lease, and committed input artifacts rather than treating the previous agent's free text as fact. 02 · PRODUCE Candidate Artifact The agent performs bounded work and emits a typed candidate artifact. Downstream work is not runnable yet. 03 · VALIDATE Schema → Semantic → Integrity → Acceptance Validate structural parseability, then business invariants, then referenced files and evidence, and when needed verify the stage's actual acceptance criteria. 04 · COMMIT Artifact Commit + Atomic State Transition After validation, mark the artifact authoritative and commit the legal transition using CAS, a single writer, a transaction, or workflow-engine-owned state. 05 · PUBLISH Next Task Becomes Runnable Only committed state is published downstream. Failures route to repair, retry, or escalation instead of silently propagating an invalid candidate. Core ordering produce → validate → commit → publish downstream FIG. 8. S2 · STATE SEPARATION Do not collapse workflow state, artifacts, and agent context into one conversation WORKFLOW STATE Where execution is now stage · status · revision · owner · lease · retry · approval · next transitions ARTIFACT STORE What work actually exists artifact_id · version · lineage · checksum · schema · validation_status · storage_uri AGENT CONTEXT What this worker needs now prompt · retrieved context · tool results · scratch state · local plan Recovery boundary An agent process crash should not erase workflow state or validated artifacts. Recovery depends on durable state, checkpoints, or event history—not on the model remembering where it stopped. FIG. 8. S3 · FAILURE / RECOVERY MATRIX Not every failure should be described as rolling back a checkpoint Failure Preferred response Why Schema invalid repair / rerun current stage Validated upstream artifacts usually remain valid Evidence missing repair reference / rerun producer Repair from the earliest invalid artifact Worker crashed lease expiry → reconcile → reassign A dead process does not imply the side effect did not occur Stale state write reject revision / reload CAS / explicit concurrency control External side effect uncertain idempotency · reconciliation · compensation A checkpoint cannot undo the external world Repeated repair failure bounded escalation Avoid endless agent-to-agent repair loops FIG. 8. S4 · LONG-RUNNING OPERATIONS Multi-hour and multi-day workflows also need leases, version compatibility, and handoff metrics LEASE Who owns the task now? owner · lease_token · heartbeat · expires_at · reassignment VERSIONING Can old state run on new code? workflow_version · schema_version · prompt/tool/policy version · migration / pinning METRICS Is the handoff reliable? handoff failure · resume success · stale-write reject · duplicate side effect · time in stage Final rule Agents may be ephemeral; workflow state and validated artifacts must be durable. External verification date: 2026-09-28. Current LangGraph Persistence documentation supports checkpoint-based graph-state persistence and failure recovery; current Temporal Durable AI and Workflow documentation supports crash recovery from durable event history, multi-day workflows, version-aware deterministic replay, and compensation patterns. These are implementation evidence, not a claim that every system must use the same checkpoint mechanism. Cancellation, Interruption, and Steering: stop the runtime, not just the UI §8. T After the user presses stop, the runtime must answer which work belongs to this run, how cancellation propagates, what state already-started side effects are in, how the conversation protocol is repaired, and whether new input means cancel, steer, or follow up. FIG. 8. T1 · CANCELLATION SCOPE Cancellation is a hierarchical runtime signal, not a global boolean Cancelling a parent scope stops owned descendants; cancelling one child should not automatically kill siblings or the whole session. ROOT · RUN SCOPE Cancel Request → Stop New Work User cancellation, timeout, policy, supersession, or host shutdown may trigger the scope, but the reason must be preserved. MODEL Stream / Retry / Backoff abortable request · retry wait · compaction · next model call TOOLS Tool Batch / Tool Child dispatch boundary · per-tool child signal · no new calls after cancel OS / REMOTE JOB Owned Execution Tree process group · container job · browser session · remote cancel handle SUBTASK Foreground vs Detached Foreground work usually inherits the parent; background work needs an explicit independent lifetime and cancel handle. Core rule Every blocking boundary must either accept cancellation directly or race against a cancellation signal. FIG. 8. T2 · INTERRUPTED TOOL TRUTH MODEL After interruption, determine how far the tool executed before deciding to retry NOT STARTED Rejected / Cancelled Before Run No side effect occurred; repair the protocol with a cancelled/rejected result and make a new decision. STARTED · ABORTED Partial / Unknown Effect The tool started, so the runtime cannot claim it never ran; inspect files, processes, remote systems, or business state. RESULT LOST Completed? Ack Missing The remote action may have committed even though the local result was lost; reconcile before any retry. COMPLETED Trusted Result Available A complete trustworthy result is available and can be committed into conversation or workflow state normally. SIDE-EFFECT BOUNDARY Cancellation changes control flow; it does not retroactively erase side effects. TRANSCRIPT REPAIR Synthetic tool results repair the provider protocol. They must encode the real execution state rather than falsely claiming no execution merely to make the next API request valid. FIG. 8. T3 · USER CONTROL SEMANTICS Cancel, steer, and follow-up are not the same event CANCEL Terminate Current Scope Stop new work → terminate owned execution → reconcile → repair protocol → become quiescent. STEER Change Next Decision Inject at a safe action/result boundary; already-observed tool work and side effects still belong in the next decision. FOLLOW-UP Queue After Completion Start the new request only after the current run finishes its pending work—useful for 'after this, do that.' SAFE INJECTION BOUNDARY tool_use → tool_result → steering → next model call Do not inject arbitrary user messages into an unresolved tool protocol unit; first restore a coherent action/result state. Final rule Cancellation is complete only when the execution scope is quiescent and its state is trustworthy. FIG. 8. T4 · CANCELLATION LIFECYCLE The UI may show Cancelling immediately, but the runtime should not mark the run CANCELLED yet RUNNING Work Is Active CANCEL_REQUESTED Stop Launching New Work TERMINATING Abort Requests · Stop Tools · Kill Owned Jobs RECONCILING Repair Transcript · Verify Side Effects QUIESCENT CANCELLED / FAILED / HUMAN ACTION Two latencies cancel_ack_latency measures how fast the runtime acknowledges cancellation; cancel_to_quiescence_latency measures how long it takes to actually stop and return to trustworthy state. External verification date: 2026-10-06. Current OpenAI Codex source uses hierarchical CancellationToken values and, for one-shot exec cancellation, terminates the process group, waits a 50ms grace period, then force-kills remaining members. Current Pi documentation separates abort, steer, and follow-up semantics. Anthropic's current Tool Use documentation requires a complete tool_use/tool_result protocol, and its TypeScript BetaToolRunner supports AbortSignal. These are implementation evidence; the durable rules remain vendor-neutral.

Efficient routing Cheap-model retry trap Balanced Tokens per attempt 45k Includes retrieval, context, reasoning, and output Blended token price $1. 80/1M Average price after routing, not the sticker price of one model Average attempts per task 1. 4× Includes retries, repairs, and replanning Task success rate 88% Measure against real success criteria, not model self-report Cost / attempt $0. 081 Cost / task $0. 113 Cost / successful task $0. 129 LIVE COST PATH Token volume × attempts 45k tokens × 1. 4 attempts × Blended rate $1. 80 / 1M tokens ÷ Success-rate correction 88% success → $0. 129 Cost / attempt $0. 081 Cost / task $0. 113 Cost / successful task $0. 129 Interpretation: lowering model price reduces task economics only when it does not materially increase tokens, retries, or failure rate. Production systems should track success rate, total tokens, retry rate, latency, and non-token costs together. FIG. 9. C2 · COST ACCOUNTING Usage is not cost: resolve pricing first, then join task outcome Cost observability should keep how much was used separate from how that usage was priced; otherwise pricing changes, cache reads, custom models, and non-LLM components distort historical analysis. 1 · CAPTURE Usage capture Record input, output, and other usage plus subtypes such as cache_read and reasoning; tools, search APIs, and retrieval need their own metering or literal cost. 2 · PRICE Pricing resolution Resolve price by model, provider, token type, and effective date. Price specific subtypes first, then price only residual usage at the default rate to avoid double charging. 3 · JOIN Aggregate + outcome Aggregate run cost into trace and task cost, slice by model, tool, customer, version, and other metadata, then join task success to obtain actionable cost per successful task. Cost category Breakdown in the source lesson Engineering interpretation Input Prompt · text/image input · cache reads Attribute context, prompt-prefix, tool-schema, and prefill cost. Output Generated text/image · reasoning tokens Attribute output length, reasoning, and decode cost. Other Tool · retrieval · custom run Include search APIs, databases, retrieval, and other non-LLM spend so token cost is not mistaken for total task cost. CACHE READ ≠ COST HOTSPOT The lesson emphasizes that cache-read tokens are typically cheaper than regular input tokens, so a large cache-read share of input tokens does not imply a large share of input cost. Analyze token type × effective price rather than token share alone. Run type LangSmith source mechanism Reusable engineering principle LLM Token counts + ls_model_name + ls_provider + pricing table Separate usage from pricing; manually report usage when automatic extraction is unavailable. Custom / self-hosted LLM usage_metadata + custom pricing entry Token counts without a matching pricing rule provide usage but not reliable cost. Tool / API / Retrieval usage_metadata. total_cost Components without token-based unit pricing should report metered or billed literal cost before trace/task aggregation. PRICING VERSION BOUNDARY The source lesson states that LangSmith model-pricing updates are not retroactive and affect only traces logged after the change. Historical cost analysis should preserve pricing effective date/version and distinguish actual-at-the-time pricing from normalized repricing. Observation scope LangSmith Best for answering Micro Trace Tree Where did this trace or child run spend money? Aggregate Project Stats How many tokens and how much total spend does the project have? Slice / Trend Dashboard + Group by metadata Which tool, model, customer, app version, or environment drove the cost movement? ACCOUNTING RULE Measure usage separately from pricing, then join cost with task outcome. CANONICAL RULE Optimize cost per successful task, not price per model call. SOURCE EXAMPLE In the previously cited Glean comparison, the source reports roughly $0. 45/task versus $1. 84/task and about 29. 8M versus 88. 8M tokens. Treat it as a source-specific example showing how routing plus better context can reduce both blended price and token volume, not as a universal benchmark transferable to other systems. Sources: LangChain Academy · Token and Cost Breakdowns · Setting Up Cost Tracking · Viewing Costs in the UI · LangSmith Cost Tracking Docs · AI Engineering · Loop vs Graph Engineering Clearly Explained Agent Experience Learning: promote experience through explicit gates §9. X Agent self-learning is not automatic weight mutation after every task. Raw traces first pass through evaluation, root-cause analysis, distillation, and validation before being promoted into memory, skills, deterministic rules, regression datasets, or training data. FIG. 9. X1 · EXPERIENCE PROMOTION SYSTEM Turn what happened into something safe to reuse later A trace is evidence; an experience is a validated abstraction. Different lessons belong in different system layers. 01 Production Trace Record observable actions, structured decisions, tool I/O, state transitions, validation, cost, and outcome. A raw success log is not a ground-truth demonstration. 02 Eval + Root Cause First identify whether the problem came from the agent, tool, data, permissions, environment, or evaluator before deciding whether there is a reusable lesson. 03 Experience Distillation Extract triggers, recommended actions, anti-patterns, applicability, evidence, scope, version compatibility, and do-not-apply conditions. 04 Promotion Router Use stability, scope, authority, programmability, and evaluability to choose Memory, Skill, Rule, Regression, or Training. 05 Eval / Shadow / Release Experience moves from CANDIDATE to VALIDATED to SHADOW to ACTIVE. Every promotion needs versioning, evidence, rollback, and regression protection. Core rule Agent self-learning is a controlled experience-promotion system, not an uncontrolled self-modification loop. FIG. 9. X2 · WHERE SHOULD EXPERIENCE LIVE? Not every experience belongs in memory, and not every memory belongs in model weights Experience type Promotion target Why Durable user preference or time-scoped project constraint Profile / Project Memory Needs scope, expiry, and deletability Repeated validated procedure Skill / Procedure Abstract repeated cases into reusable steps Business invariant that must always hold Code / Policy / Validator Should not depend on the model remembering it Real production failure Regression Dataset The lesson must become reproducibly testable Stable repeated model-behavior gap Training Dataset Promote to SFT, preference optimization, or RL only with a clear evaluation contract FAST External-experience fast path Memory / Skill / Rule / Regression: traceable, invalidatable, and fast to update. SLOW Parameter-learning slow path Curated training data → SFT / preference / RL → full regression → model release. NEGATIVE TRANSFER Experience systems must not measure only improvement after recall; they must also detect whether retrieved or promoted lessons make previously correct tasks worse. Stale lessons, scope leakage, and self-reinforcing errors are learning risks that need monitoring. Final rule Learning is incomplete until the lesson becomes testable. Guardrail Evidence Gate + Behavior Observability §9. G Production agents need more than system-health observability. They also need behavioral evidence explaining how a task executed, while high-risk actions should bind versioned rules, immutable action snapshots, and evidence. FIG. 9. G1 · BEHAVIOR OBSERVABILITY Session → Task → Trajectory → Step → Outcome SYSTEM OBSERVABILITY Is the runtime healthy? latency · throughput · errors · resource · cost · cache · availability BEHAVIOR OBSERVABILITY Why did the task execute this way? trajectory · tool choice · state change · evidence · recovery · outcome TRACE vs TRAJECTORY Trace = operational call graph. Trajectory = task-semantic execution record. They can share trace context without being the same concept. FIG. 9. G2 · GUARDRAIL EVIDENCE GATE Spec + ChangeSet + Evidence → PASS / BLOCKED / UNKNOWN RULE GuardrailSpec@revision Pins check objectives, decision criteria, and evidence requirements. ACTION SNAPSHOT immutable ChangeSet@digest Freezes what is about to execute so the checked object cannot drift. EVIDENCE Agent Submission(s) source · observation time · scope · result · failure reason GATE PASS · BLOCKED · UNKNOWN UNKNOWN ≠ PASS. Insufficient evidence should hold or escalate, not relax the standard. COMMIT Executor revalidates current real-world state permission · resource version · target · action · duplicate risk Authority boundary Evidence collection can be delegated; authority to commit remains with the control plane.

Decode remains a separate cost. 10.1 Prefill、Decode 与两种 KV 复用 机制 复用范围 主要价值 Within-request KV Cache 同一请求已处理 token 避免 Decode 时重复计算全部历史 Cross-request Prefix Cache 不同请求之间兼容且完全相同的 token prefix 避免重复 Prefill，降低 TTFT 没有跨请求 Prefix Cache 时，相同前缀通常仍会被各自 Prefill。现代 serving engine 是否默认启用、如何索引和何时淘汰都取决于 engine、version 与 config，因此不要把“默认不能共享”当成通用事实。 10.2 Cache Hit 需要 token-level identity KEY 常见兼容条件 model / revision · tokenizer · chat template · exact token IDs · position semantics · adapter / LoRA · multimodal identity · cache namespace / salt · block granularity MISS 常见命中率杀手 动态 timestamp / request id · Tool Schema 顺序变化 · 不稳定 JSON serialization · tenant 信息过早注入 · role prompt 过早分叉 PROMPT LAYOUT Prefix Cache 的命中率部分取决于应用层 Prompt Layout。把稳定公共前缀放在前面、动态内容放在后面，通常更容易复用；但绝不能为了命中率破坏语义、权限或租户隔离。 10.3 SGLang RadixAttention vs vLLM APC Runtime Prefix 索引思路 共同目标 SGLang Radix-style prefix tree / longest-prefix reuse 复用已经计算的精确共享前缀 KV，避免重复 Prefill vLLM Block-oriented APC；使用 prefix-aware block hash 查找已计算 blocks 复用已经计算的精确共享前缀 KV，避免重复 Prefill RadixAttention 是 SGLang 的具体机制/术语，不应该当作所有 Prefix Caching 的通用名称。不同 runtime 可以使用不同数据结构达到同样的跨请求前缀复用目标。 10.4 Prefix Cache ≠ Semantic Cache Cache Key 复用什么 是否仍调用模型 KV / Prefix Cache exact compatible token prefix intermediate K/V computation 是：suffix / Decode 仍需执行 Exact Response Cache exact request key final response 通常否 Semantic Cache embedding / semantic similarity prior response / tool result 命中时可跳过 必须区分 Prefix caching reuses computation. Semantic caching reuses an answer. 10.5 Multi-Agent：先保留边界，再优化共享前缀 Common System Policy + Common Tool Schema + Stable Safety / Formatting Rules ↓ shared prefix Agent-specific Role / Skill Context ↓ divergence User / Task Context 不要为了 Cache Hit 强行让所有 Agent 使用相同角色定义。先保证责任边界、权限隔离与语义正确，再优化共享前缀。 10.6 Security：Cache sharing 也是隔离策略 SHARE 更高复用 更高 prefix hit rate · 更少 Prefill · 更低 TTFT；适合同一 trust group 内大量公共前缀。 ISOLATE 更强隔离 通过 cache namespace / salt 限制跨用户或跨租户复用，牺牲部分命中率换取隐私边界。 vLLM CACHE SALT vLLM 当前支持 request-level cache_salt，把 salt 混入 Prefix Cache key。不同 salt 的请求不能共享缓存 blocks，可用于降低跨租户 prefix timing side-channel 风险。 10.7 Serving Metrics：用 workload 证明收益 指标 回答什么问题 prefix-cache hit rate 有多少请求真正复用了公共前缀？ cached-prefix tokens / request 每次命中到底省掉多少 Prefill？ TTFT P50 / P95 / P99 首 token 延迟是否真的改善？ prefill / request throughput 释放的计算是否转化成吞吐？ KV utilization / eviction 缓存收益是否被显存压力与淘汰抵消？ cost per successful task Serving 优化最终是否改善业务单位成本？ 10.8 面试回答 回答结构 多个 Agent 能否复用 KV Cache，要看它们是否由支持 Prefix Caching 的 serving computation，不是可变会话状态。它主要优化 Prefill / TTFT，不直接减少 Decode；Semantic Cache 则是另一层的 response reuse。生产上还必须考虑 Prompt 对齐、cache eviction 和 multi-tenant isolation / cache salt。 SOURCE BOUNDARY 本章由用户提供的多 Agent KV textEn: CHAPTER 10 Inference Serving, Deployment, Security, and AI Platform SERVING · K·P·S·M W WHEN T TRADE-OFF M METRIC Agent applications ultimately run on an inference system. At the serving layer, whether multiple Agents can share KV cache is not a simple yes/no question; it depends on compatible identical token prefixes plus the inference engine's cache key, lifecycle, and isolation policy. FIG. 10. 1 · PREFIX KV REUSE Reuse computed immutable prefixes, not one mutable session cache A prefix-cache hit skips Prefill for the shared prefix only; the divergent suffix and later Decode remain request-specific. 01 Shared Prefix System Prompt · Tool Schema · Stable Policy → identical token prefix 02 Prefix Cache Lookup A radix tree, block hash, or similar mechanism finds the reusable prefix 03 Prefill Suffix Compute only the uncached Agent-specific or user-specific suffix 04 Decode Each request continues its own token-by-token generation Core boundary Prefix caching primarily reduces Prefill / TTFT; Decode remains a separate cost. 10. 1 Prefill, Decode, and two kinds of KV reuse Mechanism Reuse scope Primary value Within-request KV Cache Past tokens in the same request Avoid recomputing the full history during Decode Cross-request Prefix Cache Compatible identical token prefixes across requests Avoid redundant Prefill and reduce TTFT Without cross-request prefix caching, identical prefixes are typically prefilled separately. Whether modern serving engines enable it by default, how they index it, and when they evict entries depend on the engine, version, and configuration, so 'sharing is disabled by default' is not a universal fact. 10. 2 Cache hits require token-level identity KEY Typical compatibility factors model / revision · tokenizer · chat template · exact token IDs · position semantics · adapter / LoRA · multimodal identity · cache namespace / salt · block granularity MISS Common hit-rate killers dynamic timestamps / request IDs · changing tool-schema order · unstable JSON serialization · tenant data inserted too early · early role-specific divergence PROMPT LAYOUT Prefix-cache hit rate is partly an application prompt-layout property. Stable common prefixes placed earlier and dynamic content later are usually easier to reuse, but cache efficiency must never override semantics, authorization, or tenant isolation. 10. 3 SGLang RadixAttention vs vLLM APC Runtime Prefix indexing approach Shared goal SGLang Radix-style prefix tree / longest-prefix reuse Reuse already-computed KV for exact shared prefixes and avoid redundant Prefill vLLM Block-oriented APC with prefix-aware block hashes Reuse already-computed KV for exact shared prefixes and avoid redundant Prefill RadixAttention is an SGLang-specific mechanism and term, not the generic name for all prefix caching. Different runtimes can use different data structures to achieve the same cross-request prefix-reuse goal. 10. 4 Prefix Cache ≠ Semantic Cache Cache Key What is reused Model call after hit? KV / Prefix Cache exact compatible token prefix intermediate K/V computation Yes: suffix / Decode still run Exact Response Cache exact request key final response Usually no Semantic Cache embedding / semantic similarity prior response / tool result Can be skipped on hit Must distinguish Prefix caching reuses computation. Semantic caching reuses an answer. 10. 5 Multi-Agent: preserve boundaries first, then optimize shared prefixes Common System Policy + Common Tool Schema + Stable Safety / Formatting Rules ↓ shared prefix Agent-specific Role / Skill Context ↓ divergence User / Task Context Do not force all Agents to share one role definition merely to improve cache hits. Preserve responsibility boundaries, permission isolation, and semantic correctness first; optimize shared prefixes second. 10. 6 Security: cache sharing is also an isolation policy SHARE More sharing Higher prefix hit rate · less Prefill · lower TTFT; useful when a trust group legitimately shares common prefixes. ISOLATE Stronger isolation Use cache namespaces or salts to restrict cross-user or cross-tenant reuse, trading some hit rate for privacy isolation. vLLM CACHE SALT vLLM currently supports request-level cache_salt, mixing the salt into prefix-cache keys. Requests with different salts cannot share cached blocks, reducing cross-tenant prefix timing side-channel risk. 10. 7 Serving metrics: prove value with workload evidence Metric Question answered prefix-cache hit rate How many requests actually reused a common prefix? cached-prefix tokens / request How much Prefill does each hit avoid? TTFT P50 / P95 / P99 Did first-token latency actually improve? prefill / request throughput Did saved computation translate into throughput? KV utilization / eviction Are cache benefits offset by memory pressure and eviction? cost per successful task Did serving optimization improve business unit economics? 10. 8 Interview answer Answer structure Whether multiple Agents can reuse KV cache depends on whether they are served by an engine with prefix caching and whether their requests share a compatible identical token prefix. Without cross-request prefix caching, Prefill is repeated; with mechanisms such as SGLang's radix-style cache or vLLM APC, later requests can reuse cached KV blocks for the shared prefix and compute only the divergent suffix. What is shared is immutable prefix computation, not mutable session state. This primarily optimizes Prefill and TTFT, not Decode; semantic caching is a separate response-reuse layer.
